meta.name: Juniper Networks Certified Associate Junos (JNCIA-Junos JN0-105)
meta.notes: Initial JNCIA-Junos pack — covers Junos OS architecture (Routing Engine vs Packet Forwarding Engine), candidate vs active configuration with commit semantics, CLI operational vs configuration mode, user-authentication classes, static and dynamic routing basics, route preference, firewall filters (stateless ACLs), interface naming and unit semantics, Junos protocol-independent properties, VLANs and trunk encapsulation, and Class-of-Service fundamentals. Balanced answer key (3/3/3/3). v1.1: +10 — commit check, show|compare, run prefix, CLI help, static default route, preference order, PFE transit vs exception traffic, active-route marker, load override, software upgrade.

questions.question: Which two software components of the Junos OS architecture are separated to ensure that control-plane churn cannot interrupt forwarding of transit packets?
options: Routing Engine (control plane) and Packet Forwarding Engine (data plane)
J-Web GUI and the CLI shell
Candidate configuration database and the rescue configuration
Syslog daemon and the kernel
questions.explanation: Junos OS is built on a strict separation between the Routing Engine (RE), which runs the protocols and owns the master copy of the configuration, and the Packet Forwarding Engine (PFE), which forwards transit traffic against a downloaded forwarding table. Because the PFE keeps forwarding even when the RE is busy or rebooting, control-plane churn does not interrupt user traffic. J-Web and the CLI are both management interfaces sitting on top of the RE, candidate vs rescue configs are two configuration databases on the RE, and syslog/kernel are RE-internal services — none of those pairs describe the control- vs data-plane split.

questions.question: You have typed several `set` statements while in configuration mode but have not yet activated them. Which Junos configuration database currently holds those changes?
options: Active configuration (running on the device)
Rescue configuration (manual snapshot)
Candidate configuration (staged, not yet applied)
Rollback 0 (previous active configuration)
questions.explanation: Junos uses a candidate configuration as a scratchpad: every `set`, `delete` or `edit` you issue in configuration mode edits this candidate, not the running device. Nothing takes effect until you `commit`, at which point the candidate becomes the new active configuration and the previous active is pushed onto the rollback stack as rollback 1. The rescue configuration is a user-selected snapshot restored with `rollback rescue`, the active configuration is what is currently running, and rollback 0 is the active configuration itself (the file you just committed).

questions.question: Which Junos command applies the staged candidate configuration but reverts it automatically after 10 minutes unless a follow-up command is issued?
options: commit synchronize
commit and-quit
commit check
commit confirmed 10
questions.explanation: `commit confirmed <minutes>` activates the candidate immediately but starts a timer; if you do not issue a plain `commit` within that window the device automatically rolls back to the previous configuration. This protects against locking yourself out after a risky change. `commit check` only validates syntax without activating anything, `commit synchronize` pushes the configuration to both Routing Engines on a dual-RE chassis, and `commit and-quit` activates the configuration and leaves configuration mode but provides no auto-revert.

questions.question: Which Junos login class permission grants full read-write access to every hierarchy and lets the user execute all commands?
options: operator
read-only
super-user
unauthorized
questions.explanation: Junos ships four predefined login classes. `super-user` carries all permission bits (`all`), so a user in that class can both view and modify any hierarchy and execute every operational command. `operator` allows operational-mode tasks such as clearing interfaces but cannot change configuration, `read-only` can only view configuration and operational state, and `unauthorized` cannot log in at all. Custom classes can be built with a subset of permission flags when finer-grained control is needed.

questions.question: On a Juniper MX router an interface is shown as `ge-0/2/3.0`. What does the `.0` at the end of that name represent?
options: Slot number on the FPC where the PIC is installed
PIC number inside the slot
Loopback instance index
Logical unit (sub-interface) carrying protocol family configuration
questions.explanation: Junos interface names follow `<media>-<fpc>/<pic>/<port>.<unit>`. For `ge-0/2/3.0`, ge is Gigabit Ethernet, 0 is the FPC slot, 2 is the PIC, 3 is the port and the trailing `.0` is the logical unit number. Protocol families (`family inet`, `family inet6`, VLAN tags, MPLS, etc.) are always configured under a unit, not directly on the physical port, so every usable interface needs at least unit 0. Loopback uses `lo0.<unit>`, not the trailing field of a transit interface.

questions.question: A Junos router has learned the same prefix 10.20.0.0/16 from OSPF (route preference 10) and from a static route (route preference 5). Which route is installed in the forwarding table, and why?
options: The OSPF route, because dynamic protocols always win over static
The static route, because its route preference value is lower
Both routes are installed and traffic is load-balanced 50/50 by default
Neither — Junos rejects the conflict until one source is withdrawn
questions.explanation: Junos selects the route with the lowest route preference (its equivalent of administrative distance). Static routes default to preference 5 and internal OSPF routes default to preference 10, so the static route wins and is installed in the forwarding table; the OSPF route stays as a backup in the routing table marked hidden by the active flag of the static. Load-balancing only happens between routes of equal preference (and equal metric) when `per-packet`/`per-flow` load balancing is enabled via a routing policy.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a stateless firewall filter in Junos OS?
options: It tracks TCP connection state and only allows return traffic for established sessions
It performs deep packet inspection up through layer 7 of the OSI model
It evaluates each packet independently against `from`/`then` terms based on header fields
It is applied only on the loopback interface to filter Routing Engine traffic
questions.explanation: Junos stateless firewall filters (analogous to ACLs on other platforms) are made of ordered terms, each with `from` match conditions on header fields (addresses, ports, protocol, DSCP, etc.) and a `then` action (`accept`, `discard`, `reject`, `count`, `policer`). Each packet is judged on its own — there is no session table — which is why they are called stateless. Connection tracking, return-flow inspection and L7 inspection are jobs for the SRX stateful security policy, not stateless filters. Stateless filters can be applied on any interface, including the lo0 interface to protect the Routing Engine, but their use is not restricted to lo0.

questions.question: Which Junos OS service is described as a protocol-independent property — meaning it can act on routes regardless of which routing protocol learned them?
options: OSPF area 0 backbone summarization
BGP attribute manipulation inside a peer group
PIM rendezvous-point election
Routing policy that imports or exports routes between the routing table and protocols
questions.explanation: Junos routing policy and routing options (aggregate, generated, static, martians, autonomous-system) are configured under `[edit routing-options]` and `[edit policy-options]`, and they apply to the routing table regardless of where a route was learned. The same policy framework filters BGP advertisements, OSPF redistribution and static-to-IS-IS leaks alike. OSPF summarization, BGP attribute changes and PIM RP election are all features of specific routing protocols, so they are by definition protocol-dependent, not protocol-independent.

questions.question: On a Junos EX Series switch interface configured for trunk mode, which type of frames are sent untagged by default?
options: Frames belonging to the configured native VLAN ID
All multicast and broadcast frames regardless of VLAN
Only frames in VLAN 1 (which cannot be changed)
No frames — every frame on a trunk port is always 802.1Q tagged
questions.explanation: On a Junos trunk port the configured native VLAN (`native-vlan-id` under the interface) is transmitted and accepted untagged, while every other VLAN carried on the trunk is 802.1Q-tagged. This matches the IEEE 802.1Q behaviour used by other vendors and lets a trunk interoperate with hosts or legacy switches that do not tag. The native VLAN is configurable per port (not fixed to VLAN 1), broadcast/multicast frames are tagged according to the VLAN they belong to, and saying that everything is always tagged would defeat the purpose of having a native VLAN.

questions.question: Which operational-mode command displays a summary of every interface on a Junos device along with its admin and link status?
options: show configuration interfaces
show interfaces terse
monitor traffic interface
request system halt
questions.explanation: `show interfaces terse` is the go-to one-line-per-interface summary in operational mode: it prints the interface name, admin status, link status, and any configured protocol families with their addresses. `show configuration interfaces` shows configured statements, not live status. `monitor traffic interface` is the Junos tcpdump-equivalent used to capture transit packets. `request system halt` shuts the device down — a destructive command that has nothing to do with viewing interface status.

questions.question: How many forwarding classes does Junos OS support by default, and what is each one mapped to in the Class-of-Service framework?
options: Two forwarding classes, mapped to two output queues (high and low priority)
Four forwarding classes (best-effort, expedited-forwarding, assured-forwarding, network-control), each mapped to its own queue
Eight forwarding classes, all mapped to a single shared queue and prioritized purely by DSCP
Zero — forwarding classes do not exist until you configure a custom CoS profile
questions.explanation: Out of the box Junos defines four forwarding classes — best-effort, expedited-forwarding, assured-forwarding, and network-control — each mapped to one of four output queues (0 through 3) on the egress interface. You can extend the model (up to 8 or 16 queues depending on the platform) but the default four-class, four-queue layout is what JNCIA-Junos expects you to know. The two- and zero-class options are simply wrong, and mapping every class to the same queue would defeat the purpose of differentiated service.

questions.question: After committing a configuration that you suspect broke OSPF, which Junos command returns the device to the configuration that was active immediately before that commit?
options: rollback 1 then commit
load override terminal
request system reboot
clear ospf neighbor all
questions.explanation: Junos keeps the previous active configurations on a numbered rollback stack — rollback 0 is the current active, rollback 1 is the one immediately before it, up to rollback 49 on most platforms. Entering configuration mode and typing `rollback 1` loads that previous configuration into the candidate; you then `commit` to make it active. `load override terminal` reads a brand-new configuration from your paste buffer (not from history), `request system reboot` restarts the device (which would simply reload the broken active config), and `clear ospf neighbor all` only resets OSPF adjacencies without reversing the configuration change.

questions.question: Before activating a staged configuration, you want Junos to validate its syntax and consistency without applying anything to the running device. Which command does this?
options: commit confirmed
commit synchronize
commit check
commit and-quit
questions.explanation: `commit check` validates the candidate configuration — syntax, references, constraint checks — and reports errors without activating it. `commit confirmed` activates with an automatic rollback timer; `commit synchronize` commits on both Routing Engines of a dual-RE system; `commit and-quit` activates and drops you back to operational mode.

questions.question: While in configuration mode you have staged several changes. Which command shows exactly what differs between the candidate configuration and the active configuration?
options: show configuration | display set
show | compare
show system commit
show | display inheritance
questions.explanation: `show | compare` (run from configuration mode) renders a patch-style diff between the candidate and the active (running) configuration, with `+` and `-` line markers. `show configuration | display set` prints the active config as set commands; `show system commit` lists commit history; `| display inheritance` expands configuration groups, not differences.

questions.question: You are in configuration mode editing an interface and need to check reachability with ping without losing your place in the hierarchy. What is the most efficient way to do this?
options: Type `exit` repeatedly to reach operational mode, ping, then navigate back to the interface hierarchy
Open a second SSH session, because operational commands can never be issued while a candidate configuration exists
Prefix the operational command: `run ping 10.0.0.1`
Commit the candidate first, since Junos blocks all operational commands while uncommitted changes are staged
questions.explanation: The `run` prefix executes any operational-mode command from inside configuration mode — `run ping`, `run show route`, `run show interfaces terse` — without leaving the hierarchy or touching the candidate. Exiting and returning works but is slow; Junos does not block operational commands while changes are staged, so the other options rest on false premises.

questions.question: Which command creates a static default route in Junos that sends all unmatched traffic to the gateway 192.0.2.1?
options: set routing-options static route 0.0.0.0/0 next-hop 192.0.2.1
set protocols static default gateway 192.0.2.1
set system default-route next-hop 192.0.2.1
questions.explanation: Static routes in Junos live under the `routing-options` hierarchy: `set routing-options static route 0.0.0.0/0 next-hop 192.0.2.1`. The `ip route` syntax is Cisco IOS, a frequent distractor on this exam; static routing is not configured under `protocols`, and there is no `system default-route` statement.

questions.question: A Junos router learns the prefix 172.16.0.0/16 from a static route, from OSPF internal, and from BGP. Using default route preference values, which source is installed as the active route?
options: BGP, because external routing information always wins over locally configured routes
OSPF, because link-state protocols are always preferred over static configuration
The static route, because its default preference (5) is numerically lowest
All three are installed and the router load-balances across them equally
questions.explanation: Junos selects the route source with the lowest preference value: static routes default to 5, OSPF internal to 10, and BGP to 170. The static route therefore becomes active. Lower-preference wins is the opposite intuition of 'bigger is better' and is a standard JNCIA test point; equal-cost load balancing only applies to multiple routes from the same protocol at the same preference and metric.

questions.question: On a Junos router, which type of traffic is processed by the Packet Forwarding Engine WITHOUT involving the Routing Engine?
options: An SSH session terminating on the router's management interface
Transit packets being forwarded from one interface to another
Routing protocol updates such as OSPF hellos addressed to the router
Ping packets whose destination is one of the router's own addresses
questions.explanation: The PFE forwards transit traffic in hardware using its copy of the forwarding table; the RE is not in the data path. Traffic addressed to the router itself — SSH to the management plane, routing protocol packets, pings to local addresses — is exception (host-bound) traffic punted to the Routing Engine. Separating these planes is the core of the Junos architecture.

questions.question: In the output of `show route`, what does an asterisk (*) next to a route entry indicate?
options: The route has been manually pinned by an operator and cannot be replaced
The route is hidden and excluded from the forwarding table until its next hop resolves
The route is currently active and is the one installed in the forwarding table
The route was learned within the last 60 seconds and is still being verified
questions.explanation: The asterisk marks the active route — the entry chosen among all sources for that prefix and pushed to the forwarding table. Hidden routes are shown by `show route hidden` and carry no asterisk; Junos has no concept of operator-pinned or probation routes in this display.

questions.question: You have a saved configuration file and want to completely replace the candidate configuration with the file's contents before committing. Which command do you use?
options: load merge /var/tmp/golden.conf
load override /var/tmp/golden.conf
load set /var/tmp/golden.conf
load replace /var/tmp/golden.conf
questions.explanation: `load override` discards the entire candidate and substitutes the file's contents — the full-replacement operation. `load merge` adds the file's statements on top of the existing candidate; `load set` reads a file of set/delete commands and applies them line by line; `load replace` substitutes only the hierarchies marked with `replace:` tags in the file.

questions.question: While typing a command, a Junos operator presses the `?` key after `show interfaces`. What does the CLI do?
options: Lists the possible completions and options valid at that point in the command hierarchy
Executes the command immediately with default arguments applied to every interface
Opens the full Junos manual page for the show interfaces command family in a pager
Inserts a literal question-mark character into the command line for use in regular expressions
questions.explanation: Context-sensitive help is built into the Junos CLI: `?` at any point lists the keywords, options and arguments valid at that position, with one-line descriptions. It does not execute anything or open manuals. (Spacebar and Tab complete partially typed keywords — another JNCIA staple.)

questions.question: Which command begins the installation of a new Junos OS software package on a device?
options: copy tftp flash followed by boot system flash
set system software upgrade package jinstall.tgz
request system software add jinstall.tgz
install junos package jinstall.tgz commit
questions.explanation: Software operations in Junos are operational-mode `request` commands: `request system software add <package>` validates and installs the package, typically followed by `request system reboot`. `copy tftp flash` is Cisco IOS practice; software installation is not a configuration statement, so no `set` syntax applies; there is no `install junos` command.
